title: Stability response notebook — API failure procedures
body:
Purpose: quick, pragmatic operator notebook for common API degradations. This is intentionally lightweight — a living lab doc for oncall responders and engineers debugging recurring failure classes: timeouts, 429s (throttling/backpressure), degraded streaming (partial chunks, stalls), and sudden elevation in 5xx/error rates. Not a governance doc; use it during incident until we extract a formal playbook.

Scope & assumptions:
- Applies to hosted inference API fronted by edge gateways and routed to serving-runtime (pool of dedicated & shared workers).
- Metrics referenced are from Prometheus/Grafana and Logs from Loki/ELK; traces in Jaeger/Tempo.
- Default SLOs: 99th percentile request latency < 300ms (short requests), streaming tail latency < 1s per-chunk, error rate < 0.5% over 5m window.

Signals that should trigger this flow (fast checks):
- 5m error rate > 0.5% AND spike vs baseline > 3x
- 95th/99th latency climbs above configured threshold for > 3m
- Surge in 429 counts (clients or upstream) or quota triggers in Console
- Streaming sessions showing incomplete chunks or client-observed stalls (support tickets, synthetic checks failing)

Quick-response checklist (first 10 min):
- Announce: slack #sre-oncall "Investigating API degradation — claiming incident" + tag pager.
- Snapshot dashboards: save links + time window. Grafana: API-overview, routing-latency, error-breakdown, streaming-health, capacity-utilization.
- Short-circuit: toggle maintenance-mode on non-critical customer routes (Console -> Route controls) if possible.
- If request backlog high, raise global throttling on host gateway to shed non-urgent traffic (edge-config: set reject-429 threshold to X%).
- Collect sample traces: run jager query for traces with status>=500 and high latency; dump 10 most recent.
- Reproduce locally: curl a failing endpoint with ?debug=true (when safe) to capture headers, body.

Investigation primitives (what to look for):
- Infrastructure vs application: are node CPU/GPU load and cgroup OOM events elevated? Check node-exporter, nvidia-smi logs.
- Queue/backlog: inspect request queue length in runtime (metric: runtime.request_queue_depth). Long queues => slow backend or mis-sized worker pools.
- KV cache/evictions: large KV miss rate can spike per-token cost & latency. Metric: runtime.kv_cache_hit_ratio.< 60% suggests cold cache.
- Batching anomalies: look at batch size distribution. Sudden large batches increase tail latency. Metric: runtime.batch_size_p50/p95.
- Model variant failures: fallback to quantized/compat variants may be misconfigured. Check routing logs for fallback kick-ins.
- External dependencies: auth, billing, KMS timeouts can surface as 500s in frontends.

Mitigations by failure type (practical steps):
- Timeouts (individual request latency high, clients time out):
  1) Identify slow path: use traces to find span with largest latency (model inference, compilation, kernel stall).
  2) If model inference is slow and CPU/GPU healthy: reduce batch target (runtime config) for the affected model to favor latency. Command: POST /admin/runtime/configs/<model>/update {"batch_target": 1} (use Console or admin API).
  3) If GPU utilization saturated: scale up pool temporarily (Dedicated: request burst or spin extra nodes) or route to lower-cost region where spare capacity exists.
  4) If KV cache cold: prioritize warmup by running synthetic warmup traffic for top prefixes (script: tools/warmup/warm-prefixes.sh).
  5) If short spike, enable short-lived request-level queue timeouts to fail fast and protect workers: set gateway.request_timeout=3s.

- 429s (client-side rate limiting or upstream backpressure):
  1) Check where 429s originate: gateway vs runtime vs rate-limiter service. Drilldown metric: response.code_origin (gateway/runtime).
  2) If gateway is rejecting: inspect recent config changes (edge deploys in last 30m). Rollback if suspect.
  3) If runtime rejecting due to overload: increase concurrency limit for higher-tier customers only, or enact per-route circuit breaker to protect system.
  4) Communicate to clients via status page & Slack with ETA and guidance (retry-after semantics).
  5) Short term: open fallback route mapped to a smaller model variant (lower latency/cost) for high-volume front doors. Update routing policy with canary.

- Degraded streaming (partial content, stalls, early closes):
  1) Verify chunk delivery from runtime -> gateway: check streaming success counters (stream.chunk_sent, stream.chunk_ack).
  2) If chunks generated but not sent: gateway backpressure or connection limits. Check proxy limits and keepalive settings.
  3) If runtime stalls mid-session: check KV cache usage and autorelease of session tokens; inspect runtime logs for incremental generation errors.
  4) As workaround: force stream to non-chunked mode (single-response) for affected routes for short window, if payload size allows.
  5) For WebSocket issues, rotate edge nodes serving sticky sessions or shift traffic to HTTP/2 streaming endpoints.

- Elevated 5xx/error rates (broad class):
  1) Roll forward quick triage: are errors concentrated by model, region, client, or route? Use filter in errors dashboard.
  2) If concentrated to one model: pull that model out of rotation (admin API -> set weight=0) and route to next compatible variant.
  3) If widespread: check ingress auth, service mesh control plane (mTLS cert expiry), and dependency outages (KMS, metadata services).
  4) If deployment suspect: revert last deploys (console release history) for edge or runtime. Keep a single change minimal to isolate.
  5) If due to resource exhaustion: preemptively enable emergency autoscale and deprioritize low-tier traffic.

Operator tricks & quick queries:
- PromQL snippets to run in Grafana: rate(http_requests_total{job=\"api-gateway\",status=~\"5..\"}[5m]) / rate(http_requests_total{job=\"api-gateway\"}[5m]) as error_ratio
- Top offending routes: topk(10, sum by (route) (rate(http_requests_total{status=~\"5..\"}[5m])))
- Check runtime queue: max(runtime_request_queue_depth{model=~\".*\"}) by (model)
- Tail logs: kubectl -n serving logs -l app=runtime --since=10m | grep -i error --context=3

Communication & escalation (practical):
- For customer-impacting incidents: update Statuspage with short note + affected endpoints. Keep message simple: "We are investigating elevated errors for inference API in <region>."
- Provide ETA for next update: 15m initially. Use squad runbook channel to coordinate engineers.
- If impact > 30% of requests or > 30 minutes, escalate to oncall manager and paging for product/solutions engineering.

Post-incident follow-up (postmortem checklist):
- Capture timeline with artifacts: dashboard snapshots, traces, config changes, rollout ids.
- Root-cause hypothesis and what we changed to mitigate at the time.
- Action items: owner + due date (e.g., increase default batch targets, add synthetic streaming probe, tune gateway queue length).
- Add automated alert to catch the root metric earlier (reduce SLO burn window).

Known gaps / TODOs (work-in-progress):
- Better synthetic streaming probes (end-to-end) — currently only cover short seq lengths.
- More granular origin tagging on 429s allowing route->model->instance mapping for faster triage.
- Playbooks for mixed-failure scenarios (timeouts + 429s together).

Notes to self / field tips:
- When in doubt: remove one variable at a time. e.g., pull model out of rotation before scaling cluster — it isolates surface area.
- Keep rollback fast: practice one-button rollback in staging once a quarter.
- Save a canonical set of curl headers we can paste to reproduce client behavior (Auth, Accept, X-Request-ID).

Appendix: quick commands (sane defaults)
- Admin API: curl -X POST -H \"Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN\" https://admin.redwood.ai/runtime/models/<model>/actions -d '{"drain":true}'
- Warmup script: ./tools/warmup/warm-prefixes.sh --model gpt-4-lite --count 200
- Emergency scale (k8s HPA shortcut): kubectl -n serving scale deploy/runtime-xxxx --replicas=10

Open questions to discuss in retro:
- Should we expand per-route SLA tiers with automatic circuit breakers? Pros/cons and UX for customers.
- Default batch_target of 4 seems high for latency-sensitive routes; propose dynamic policy based on route SLO.

References and leads:
- Diego: responsible for streaming infra improvements (see linked PR: https://github.com/redwood/repo/pull/1142).
- Maya: working on synthetic probes (jira: SRE-3988).
- Liam: gateway throttling and config rollback owner.

End — keep this doc short and mutate it liberally. This is the place to paste snippets that helped during the incident.

Unresolved/notes-in-progress: sample trace exports attached in incident folder (drive link placeholder), need to standardize trace retention to 14 days for faster root cause follow-up.
